annotation.title_clean: Grounding Robot Navigation in Self-Defense Law
annotation.title_en: Grounding Robot Navigation in Self-Defense Law
annotation.authors_or_issuer: Zhu, J.; Shrivastava, A.; Johnson, A.M.
annotation.summary_en: Robotics preprint analysing how U.S. self-defense law could justify humans using force against public ground robots, including when they merely perceive a threat. It synthesises law, HRI and path-planning literature and gives four recommendations for robot design, research, industry and policy, illustrated by hypothetical navigation scenarios.
key_provisions_or_claims: U.S. self-defense law rests on reasonable belief of imminent harm and a proportional response.
Perceived threat from a robot can suffice to justify human self-defense, even if the robot is safe.
Non-expert non-user bystanders are most likely to feel threatened by public ground robots.
Current robot navigation and planning methods insufficiently consider self-defense scenarios.
Four recommendations for roboticists spanning research, industry and policy, including concurrent explanations and legible behaviour.
